stem: A custom generic test is defined as `{% test positive_values(model, column_name) %} SELECT * FROM {{ model }} WHERE {{ column_name }} <= 0 {% endtest %}`, and used in `schema.yml` against several columns across several models. The team needs to confirm what makes this test genuinely reusable across all of them. What's the key mechanism?

option_texts.A: The macro's two arguments are templated into the query, so dbt passes in the right values for whichever column and model the test is attached to
option_texts.B: The test name `positive_values` must exactly match the file name it's saved in, which is what makes it reusable
option_texts.C: Generic tests are reusable because dbt automatically runs them against every column in the project, not just the ones they're attached to
option_texts.D: The test is only reusable because it happens to use `<=` instead of `<`, which dbt treats as a generic comparison

drill_answer_short: model and column_name are templated into the query, letting the same test macro apply anywhere
decision_hinge: A generic data test is defined in a test block, which contains a parameterized query and accepts arguments. There are two arguments, model and column_name, which are then templated into the query. This is what makes the data test generic.

plausible_options.C: used in `schema.yml` against several columns across several models

eliminated_by.B: used in `schema.yml` against several columns across several models
eliminated_by.D: used in `schema.yml` against several columns across several models

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — a generic test's name has no required relationship to its containing file's name
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — dbt only runs a generic test where it is explicitly attached as a property, not on every column automatically
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt does not treat any particular SQL comparison operator as inherently generic

stem: A custom generic test is defined with `{% test minimum_row_count(model, min_row_count) %} {{ config(severity = 'warn') }} SELECT COUNT(*) as cnt FROM {{ model }} ... {% endtest %}`. It is then attached to a specific model in `schema.yml` with `config: severity: error` at the usage site. The team needs to know which severity actually applies for that one usage. Which wins, and why?

option_texts.A: `error`, because a config set at the point where the test is used overrides the default baked into the test block's own definition
option_texts.B: `warn`, because a `config()` call inside the test's own macro body always wins over any later usage-site override
option_texts.C: Neither; setting severity in two places for the same test is a parse error
option_texts.D: `error`, but only because `min_row_count` was also explicitly passed as an argument

drill_answer_short: A usage-site config overrides the default severity set inside the test block's own definition
decision_hinge: Set the default for all instances of a custom generic test by setting the config inside its test block. Configure a specific instance of a generic test with its own config at the usage site.

plausible_options.B: It is then attached to a specific model in `schema.yml` with `config: severity: error` at the usage site

eliminated_by.C: It is then attached to a specific model in `schema.yml` with `config: severity: error` at the usage site
eliminated_by.D: It is then attached to a specific model in `schema.yml` with `config: severity: error` at the usage site

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the config inside the test block sets the default, not a value that overrides a more specific usage-site config
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — setting a default inside the test block and a specific override at the usage site is exactly the documented pattern, not an error
distractor_traps.D: T8: scope error — which argument is passed to the test has no bearing on which severity config wins

stem: A team wants to run just the unit tests in their dbt project, skipping data tests like `not_null` or `unique` in the same invocation. The team needs the exact command that achieves this scope. Which command is correct?

option_texts.B: `dbt test --select test_type:data`, which inverts to select only unit tests by exclusion
option_texts.C: `dbt build --select resource_type:unit_test`, since unit tests only run under `dbt build`
option_texts.D: `dbt test`, since `dbt test` already excludes data tests by default

drill_answer_short: dbt test --select test_type:unit runs only unit tests
decision_hinge: To run only your unit tests, use the command: dbt test --select test_type:unit.

eliminated_by.B: skipping data tests like `not_null` or `unique` in the same invocation

C.signal: skipping data tests like `not_null` or `unique` in the same invocation
C.requires_fact: To run only your unit tests, use the command: dbt test --select test_type:unit, which runs under dbt test rather than dbt build.

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — test_type:data is not documented as an inverting selector for unit tests
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — dbt test, not only dbt build, is the documented way to run unit tests; resource_type:unit_test is not the documented selector
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — plain dbt test runs both data tests and unit tests by default, it does not exclude either

plausible_options.D: skipping data tests like `not_null` or `unique` in the same invocation

stem: A team writes `SELECT * FROM {{ ref('dim_listings_cleansed') }} l INNER JOIN {{ ref('fct_reviews') }} r USING (listing_id) WHERE l.updated_at < r.review_date` in a `tests/` file, as a one-off consistency check between exactly these two models, not meant to be reused anywhere else. They need to know what kind of test this is, and whether it needs a `test` block to be valid.

option_texts.A: A singular data test; it needs no `test` block at all, since it's just a raw SQL query returning failing rows
option_texts.B: A generic data test; any file that joins two models via `ref()` must be wrapped in `{% test %}...{% endtest %}`
option_texts.C: An invalid test; `ref()` can only be called once per file inside the `tests/` directory
option_texts.D: A unit test; any assertion comparing values across two different models is classified as a unit test

drill_answer_short: A one-off SQL assertion with no test block is a singular data test, even when it joins two models
decision_hinge: A singular data test is the exact SQL that will return failing records, defined in a .sql file, typically in your tests directory. You can use Jinja, including ref and source, in the test definition, just like you can when creating models.

B.signal: not meant to be reused anywhere else
B.requires_fact: A singular data test is the exact SQL that will return failing records, defined in a .sql file, needing no test block, regardless of how many models it joins.

eliminated_by.C: a one-off consistency check between exactly these two models
eliminated_by.D: a one-off consistency check between exactly these two models

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — a singular data test needs no test block at all, regardless of how many models it joins
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a singular test file can use ref() as many times as needed, exactly as a model would
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — comparing values across models in a test does not make it a unit test; unit tests validate logic against static fixtures, not live cross-model joins

stem: A team needs to decide when a singular test is genuinely the better choice over a generic test. Which TWO scenarios favor a singular test?

option_texts.A: A one-off business rule specific to exactly one model, unlikely to ever be reused elsewhere
option_texts.B: A complex assertion involving a multi-table join that doesn't fit neatly into a reusable, parameterized pattern
option_texts.C: Checking that `listing_id` is unique in a dimension model, with no duplicate values allowed
option_texts.D: Validating that a column only contains values from a short, fixed list across many different models

drill_answer_short: A one-off rule or a complex multi-table join that resists parameterization both favor a singular test
decision_hinge: Singular data tests are so easy that you may find yourself writing the same basic structure repeatedly, only changing the name of a column or model. By that point, the test isn't so singular! In that case, we recommend generic data tests.

plausible_options.C: A team needs to decide when a singular test is genuinely the better choice over a generic test

D.signal: A team needs to decide when a singular test is genuinely the better choice over a generic test
D.requires_fact: unique: this data test validates that there are no duplicate values present in a field, one of the four generic tests dbt ships out of the box.

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — uniqueness is exactly the built-in unique generic test's job, not a reason to reach for a singular test
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — a fixed-list check reused across many models is exactly what accepted_values, a generic test, is for

stem: A reviews source sets `loaded_at_field: date` and `freshness: {warn_after: {count: 1, period: hour}}`, leaving `error_after` out of the block entirely. The platform engineer needs to know whether this `warn_after` config is valid as written, and what follows from leaving `error_after` out. What's true?

option_texts.A: `warn_after` requires both `count` and `period` together, which are both present here; this reviews source can only ever warn, never error
option_texts.B: `warn_after` is invalid for this reviews source without an accompanying `error_after`; dbt requires both thresholds together
option_texts.C: This reviews source's `period` value is not valid; only `day` and `minute` are accepted period units
option_texts.D: `loaded_at_field` is ignored whenever `warn_after` is configured, since `warn_after` implies dbt uses adapter metadata instead

drill_answer_short: warn_after needs both count and period; with no error_after, the source can only warn, never error
decision_hinge: Each of warn_after and error_after requires both count and period. One or both of warn_after and error_after can be provided. If neither is set, dbt will not check freshness for that resource.

plausible_options.B: leaving `error_after` out of the block entirely

eliminated_by.C: leaving `error_after` out of the block entirely

D.requires_fact: warn_after and error_after are independent freshness thresholds; loaded_at_field names the column dbt queries, with no documented interaction disabling either threshold.

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — one or both of warn_after and error_after can be provided; neither is required to accompany the other
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — hour is a documented, valid period unit alongside day and minute
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — loaded_at_field and warn_after are independent configs; one does not disable the other

stem: A `relationships` test is configured as `- name: listing_id data_tests: - relationships: to: ref('dim_listings_cleansed') field: listing_id` on `fct_reviews`. The team needs to confirm exactly what the `field` argument names here. What does `field` point at?

option_texts.A: The column in the referenced model (`dim_listings_cleansed`) that `fct_reviews.listing_id` must have a matching value in
option_texts.B: The column on `fct_reviews` itself that the test is attached to, duplicating what the column property already specifies
option_texts.C: A foreign key constraint object on `dim_listings_cleansed` that must already exist in the warehouse before the test can run
option_texts.D: The data type that both the source and target columns must share for the check to be valid

drill_answer_short: field names the column in the referenced model that must contain a matching value
decision_hinge: relationships: each customer_id in the orders model exists as an id in the customers table. Configured as relationships: arguments: to: ref('customers'), field: id.

plausible_options.B: configured as `- name: listing_id data_tests: - relationships: to: ref('dim_listings_cleansed') field: listing_id`

eliminated_by.C: The team needs to confirm exactly what the `field` argument names here
eliminated_by.D: The team needs to confirm exactly what the `field` argument names here

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — name: identifies the column under test on the current model; field: identifies the matching column on the referenced model
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — relationships is a dbt-side SQL test, it requires no pre-existing warehouse foreign key object
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — the test checks that values match, not that the two columns share an identical declared data type
